scope.scopeNotesMd: This report compares the local R4 and R6 `StructureDefinition/NutritionOrder` artifacts and directly bound local terminology artifacts. It reports only changes owned by `NutritionOrder` local elements. Inherited changes from `Resource`, `DomainResource`, `Element`, `BackboneElement`, primitive datatypes, and shared datatype internals are excluded from `findings[]` unless the local NutritionOrder element changed its own type/path/binding/constraint.
outOfScope: Inherited `Resource` and `DomainResource` element changes such as `id`, `meta`, `implicitRules`, `language`, `text`, `contained`, `extension`, and `modifierExtension` are excluded.
Inherited `Element`/`BackboneElement` constraints and modifierExtension wording changes are excluded.

Global datatype changes for `Quantity`, `CodeableReference`, `Timing`, `markdown`, `Reference`, `Identifier`, and `Annotation` internals are excluded except where NutritionOrder changed a local element's declared type or profile.
Search parameters, operations, profiles, examples, CapabilityStatements, and implementation-guide-specific rules were not assessed.
Terminology analysis did not perform full live expansions of SNOMED or intensional value sets.

narrativeReportMd:
# NutritionOrder R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
R6 retains the `NutritionOrder` artifact identity but makes many local content-model changes. Hard R4-to-R6 breaks were found in required subject naming, requester naming, removed instantiation fields, schedule representation, product/additive modeling, enteral route/max-volume naming, fluid consistency removal, texture target naming, and the strengthened `nor-1` invariant.

## Scope
The report is scoped to local `NutritionOrder` elements in the R4 and R6 core packages. Inherited base-resource and datatype-internal changes are out of scope.

## Main migration themes
R4 instances need structural conversion, not just package-version retagging. The most common mandatory transform is `patient` to `subject`; populated optional fields require additional renames or moves. R6 also introduces richer workflow, performer, delivery-device, NutritionProduct, Group-subject, and as-needed scheduling capabilities that do not round-trip cleanly to R4.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact findings are `patient` to `subject`, schedule wrapper conversion, CodeableReference product modeling, and the removal/move of clinically meaningful nutrition details such as fluid consistency and additives.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is especially important for removed `instantiates*` semantics, fluid consistency mapping, generalized additives, product references to `NutritionProduct`, and terminology value set changes.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Several breaks could have been staged with deprecated aliases or optional replacement elements. Others, such as optional R6 additions, are forward-compatible but create unavoidable R6-to-R4 data-loss risks.

## Follow-up analysis
Terminology expansions, official ConceptMaps, narrative implementation notes, and separate reports for base artifacts/datatype internals would improve confidence for detailed migration tooling.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: R6 keeps the `NutritionOrder` resource identity but substantially redesigns several local fields. The highest-impact issues are the mandatory `patient` to `subject` rename, schedule backbone restructuring, product fields switching to `CodeableReference`, removal of protocol instantiation fields, and loss/relocation of fluid/additive/enteral details. Confidence is high for structural deltas and lower for terminology semantics because expansions and official ConceptMaps were not available.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Main migration themes: (1) direct property renames (`patient`, `orderer`, enteral route/max volume/product fields); (2) structural rewrites for schedules and product/additive representation; (3) R6-to-R4 information loss from new optional workflow, performer, device, Group-subject, and NutritionProduct reference capabilities; and (4) terminology convergence from example bindings toward preferred SNOMED-oriented value sets.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for local element presence, cardinality, type, binding-strength, and invariant changes because both R4 and R6 StructureDefinitions were present and compared directly. Confidence is medium for clinical terminology and narrative intent because official diffs, narrative implementation notes, full terminology expansions, and ConceptMaps were not available in the inspected local inputs. Inherited base-resource changes were deliberately excluded.

findings.title: Local nor-1 invariant changed from warning to error

oldState.summary: R4 had local invariant nor-1 as a warning.

constraints.human: Nutrition Order SHALL contain either Oral Diet , Supplement, or Enteral Formula class

oldState.narrativeMd: An R4 `NutritionOrder` could omit all three nutrition content groups and still avoid an error-level validation failure, although a warning was emitted.

newState.summary: R6 has the same local invariant as an error.

constraints.human: Nutrition Order SHALL contain either Oral Diet , Supplement, or Enteral Formula class

newState.narrativeMd: In R6, a `NutritionOrder` must contain at least one of `oralDiet`, `supplement`, or `enteralFormula` to pass validation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct validation-strengthening change. An instance that includes the mandatory R4 fields but omits `oralDiet`, `supplement`, and `enteralFormula` can pass R4 error-level validation but fail R6 validation.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The clinical safety risk is mostly from incomplete orders that previously reached downstream systems despite the warning.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal is reasonable: a `NutritionOrder` with none of `oralDiet`, `supplement`, or `enteralFormula` has little clinical utility. Promoting `nor-1` from warning to error is a real R4-to-R6 validation break, but the old-valid/new-invalid pattern should be sparse and the base-resource guarantee is clinically meaningful, so the break is probably justified.
justification.inferredGoal: Require every NutritionOrder to actually request diet, supplement, or enteral feeding content.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the invariant as a warning in the base resource and require strict enforcement only in profiles that need it.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking design would leave `nor-1` as a warning in the base resource and enforce the SHALL through profiles or implementation policy. That is only a partial alternative because it preserves old instances by giving up universal base validation.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves sparse historical instances, but weakens the base guarantee that a NutritionOrder contains an oral diet, supplement, or enteral formula.

evidence.detail: R4 local invariant nor-1 has severity `warning`.
evidence.quote: severity=warning; expression=oralDiet.exists() or supplement.exists() or enteralFormula.exists()

evidence.detail: R6 local invariant nor-1 has severity `error`.
evidence.quote: severity=error; expression=oralDiet.exists() or supplement.exists() or enteralFormula.exists()

examples.examplesMd: The fragment is illustrative of the local invariant only; a full migration would also rename `patient` to `subject`.

findings.narrativeMd: The local `nor-1` invariant was strengthened from warning to error. This converts an incomplete but R4 error-valid order into an R6 validation failure if none of the nutrition content groups is present.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation is affected directly. The change does not create an R6-to-R4 representation issue; it makes R6 stricter about a resource that lacks all ordered nutrition content.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Before converting, identify NutritionOrder records with no `oralDiet`, `supplement`, or `enteralFormula`. Either backfill the missing ordered content from source data, quarantine the record for manual review, or avoid treating it as a conformant R6 NutritionOrder.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A profile-level requirement would have been less disruptive, but the stronger base invariant is clinically defensible because a NutritionOrder without ordered nutrition content has limited utility.

findings.title: Mandatory `patient` renamed to mandatory `subject` and widened to Patient or Group

oldState.narrativeMd: Every conformant R4 NutritionOrder carried the subject of care in `patient`.

newState.summary: R6 requires `subject` as Reference(Patient or Group).
newState.narrativeMd: R6 generalizes the element to `subject`, allowing nutrition orders for either an individual Patient or a Group.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The elements have the same required cardinality, fulfill Request.subject/W5 subject mappings, and carry the same role with a generalized name.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is high-prevalence because `patient` was mandatory in R4. R4 JSON using `patient` is not valid R6 JSON, and generated R4 APIs that expose `.patient` must be updated to `.subject`. R6 orders for a `Group` cannot be represented in the R4 `patient` element without an extension or loss of the group subject.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Wrong or missing subject mapping can misdirect a nutrition order.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goals of allowing Group nutrition orders and aligning with workflow subject naming are reasonable. However, most or all R4-valid instances could have remained valid if R6 had kept `patient` and broadened its target/definition. Because living with the older name would still meet the main capability goal with only moderate naming cost, the mandatory property rename is not clearly justified.
justification.inferredGoal: Align NutritionOrder with the workflow subject pattern and allow group nutrition orders.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the base `patient` element, broaden its target to Patient or Group, and update its definition to cover an individual or group requiring nutrition.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design is not just a migration alias: keep `patient` as the normative element, allow Reference(Patient|Group), and clarify that it identifies the individual or group needing nutrition. The tradeoff is long-term terminology awkwardness, especially for Group, but it avoids invalidating every R4 instance that uses the required `patient` field.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves mandatory R4 JSON and typed APIs, but leaves a nonoptimal `patient` name for Group orders and diverges from the common workflow `subject` pattern.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `patient` as 1..1 Reference(Patient).
R6 defines `subject` as 1..1 Reference(Patient|Group).

examples.examplesMd: Fragments isolate the subject field. Other mandatory fields are omitted for brevity.

findings.narrativeMd: The subject of the order moved from `patient` to `subject`. Because the field is mandatory, this affects essentially every R4 NutritionOrder instance and generated model. R6 also permits `Group`, which is new subject matter rather than a simple rename.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance with `patient` and no `subject` is invalid in R6. Conversely, an R6 instance whose `subject` references `Group` cannot be losslessly represented in R4 because R4 only allows Patient in the required `patient` field.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rename `patient` to `subject` when the reference is to Patient. For R6-to-R4, reject or extension-map Group subjects unless a local policy can safely expand the group into individual patient orders.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Keeping `patient` as a deprecated alias would have preserved old JSON but would also have left the resource with two competing subject fields. The R6 design is cleaner but breaking.

findings.title: `orderer` renamed to `requester`

oldState.summary: R4 optional `orderer` identified who ordered the nutrition order.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 stored the legally responsible practitioner or practitioner role in `orderer`.

newState.summary: R6 optional `requester` carries the same requester role.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 uses the workflow-aligned name `requester` with the same reference targets.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: Definitions, cardinality, target profiles, and Request.requester mapping align.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Instances containing `orderer` must be transformed because R6 will not recognize the old property. Generated code and FHIRPath expressions using `NutritionOrder.orderer` also break.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Requester identity can affect authorization and accountability workflows.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The workflow naming goal is understandable, but this appears to be a same-role rename rather than a new capability. Retaining the R4 element name with clearer definition text would have met the semantic goal for NutritionOrder with a modest consistency tradeoff, so the break was probably avoidable.
justification.inferredGoal: Align the element name with the common Request.requester pattern.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `orderer` as the base element and clarify that it is the requester/legal ordering practitioner.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A backward-compatible R6 base design could keep `orderer` and update the definition or aliases to align it with Request.requester semantics. Adding conversion guidance or tooling is not needed to make that base design work; the main downside is carrying a resource-specific older name.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves existing instances and generated APIs, at the cost of less consistency with the broader `requester` naming pattern.

evidence.detail: R4 has optional `orderer` Reference(Practitioner|PractitionerRole).
R6 has optional `requester` Reference(Practitioner|PractitionerRole).

examples.examplesMd: The example shows the property-level transform only.

findings.narrativeMd: The optional requester role changed from `orderer` to `requester`. This is a common request-pattern rename and has no target-profile narrowing, but it is still a hard wire-format and generated-code change whenever the field is present.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 JSON with `orderer` is invalid as an R6 NutritionOrder unless transformed. R6 `requester` values can be represented in R4 as `orderer` without target loss.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map `orderer` to `requester` during R4-to-R6 conversion and update FHIRPath, search extraction, UI bindings, and authorization code that reads the requester.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The rename could have been avoided by retaining `orderer`, but the R6 name is more consistent with the workflow pattern. A transitional alias would be more compatible but less clean.

findings.title: Protocol/definition instantiation elements were removed without a local replacement

oldState.summary: R4 had three repeatable instantiation elements for FHIR or external protocols/definitions.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could link a NutritionOrder to adhered-to FHIR definitions or external protocols using `instantiatesCanonical`, `instantiatesUri`, or the broader `instantiates` URI.

newState.summary: R6 NutritionOrder has no local `instantiates*` element.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds `basedOn`, but that represents a request or plan fulfilled by the order rather than an adhered-to definition, so it is not a complete semantic replacement.

facts.note: Not equivalent; basedOn is a fulfilled plan/request, not a protocol definition reference.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Any R4 instance using these elements contains properties absent from R6. The migration is potentially lossy because the computable R6 StructureDefinition does not expose a same-semantics local element.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Loss of protocol/order set provenance can affect clinical review and CDS traceability.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The computable definitions do not show an equivalent local replacement for the R4 protocol/definition references, and `basedOn` is not the same fact. Since the removed fields were optional, retaining them would not have blocked R6 workflow additions and would have preserved R4 instances, so the removal is not clearly justified from a compatibility perspective.
justification.inferredGoal: Possibly simplify NutritionOrder and rely on workflow links or extensions for protocol provenance.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the optional `instantiates*` elements, at least as deprecated fields, or add a replacement protocol-definition element while keeping the old fields valid.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would keep `instantiatesCanonical`, `instantiatesUri`, and `instantiates` as optional deprecated elements, or introduce a clearer successor while keeping the old fields valid for a transition. The tradeoff is model clutter and some overlap with other workflow links, not a fundamental failure to meet the R6 goal.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves protocol and order-set provenance, but leaves extra optional workflow/provenance surface in the resource.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `instantiatesCanonical` 0..* canonical(ActivityDefinition|PlanDefinition).
R4 defines `instantiatesUri` 0..* uri.
R4 defines `instantiates` 0..* uri.
No R6 NutritionOrder `instantiates`, `instantiatesUri`, or `instantiatesCanonical` element was found.

examples.examplesMd: A migration can preserve this information only by a local extension, external provenance, or a non-equivalent workflow mapping.

findings.narrativeMd: R4's three `instantiates*` fields disappeared from the R6 NutritionOrder content model. These fields can be important when an order is created from an order set, guideline, or external protocol.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances containing any `instantiates*` property are invalid against the R6 StructureDefinition. The break is not only syntactic: the R6 local model lacks an obvious same-meaning target, so automatic conversion may lose provenance.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory use of `instantiates*`. If the value is actually a request or plan being fulfilled, map to `basedOn`; otherwise preserve it with a cross-version extension, Provenance, or implementation-specific field and document the policy.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This removal appears avoidable from a compatibility perspective because optional deprecated fields would not invalidate old instances. The tradeoff is a less streamlined R6 resource.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Human review is needed to decide whether a given R4 instantiation URI is equivalent to R6 `basedOn` or must be preserved separately.

findings.title: Oral, supplement, and enteral schedules changed from direct Timing to schedule backbones

oldState.summary: R4 schedule elements were direct `Timing` values.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 represented oral diet and supplement schedules as repeating `Timing` arrays and enteral administration schedule as a single `Timing`.

newState.summary: R6 schedule elements are 0..1 BackboneElement wrappers with repeatable `timing` and optional as-needed fields.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 wraps timing in a schedule backbone and adds `asNeeded`/`asNeededFor` to oral, supplement, and enteral administration schedules.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 JSON places `Timing` fields directly at `schedule`; R6 expects a backbone object containing `timing`. This breaks parsers, serializers, generated classes, and FHIRPath expressions. R6 as-needed schedule semantics are not directly representable in R4.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Scheduling changes can affect when nutrition is delivered.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Supporting as-needed nutrition scheduling is a reasonable R6 goal, but wrapping every populated `schedule` in a new backbone is not the only way to reach it. Optional sibling qualifiers would preserve old Timing arrays while adding the new as-needed semantics, so the wire-format break was probably avoidable.
justification.inferredGoal: Allow schedules to carry both Timing and as-needed conditions.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the existing `schedule` Timing shape and add optional `asNeeded` and `asNeededFor` siblings at the affected scheduling locations.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could leave `oralDiet.schedule`, `supplement.schedule`, and `enteralFormula.administration.schedule` as Timing elements and add `asNeeded`/`asNeededFor` alongside them. That design is less tidy than the R6 wrapper, but it avoids a structural transform for all existing schedules and has only moderate long-term tradeoff.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 schedule JSON, but splits schedule qualifiers across siblings instead of one cohesive backbone.

evidence.detail: R4 oral diet schedule is 0..* Timing.
R6 oral diet schedule is 0..1 BackboneElement with `timing` 0..*.
R4 supplement schedule is 0..* Timing.
R6 supplement schedule is 0..1 BackboneElement with `timing` 0..*.
R4 enteral administration schedule is 0..1 Timing.
R6 enteral administration schedule is a BackboneElement with `timing`, `asNeeded`, and `asNeededFor`.

examples.examplesMd: The R6 example shows schedule semantics with no direct R4 element.

findings.narrativeMd: Schedule content was wrapped in new backbone elements. Existing R4 schedule JSON must be structurally rewritten, not just copied, and R6 adds new as-needed scheduling semantics.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with direct `Timing` schedules are invalid in R6 because fields such as `repeat` are no longer children of `schedule`; they are children of `schedule.timing`. R6 `asNeeded` and `asNeededFor` have no R4 schedule equivalent.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For oral diet and supplement, move each R4 `schedule[]` Timing into R6 `schedule.timing[]`. For enteral administration, wrap the R4 single `schedule` Timing as `schedule.timing[0]`. For R6-to-R4, preserve `asNeeded` information with extensions or manual review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change could have been less disruptive by adding optional as-needed fields alongside the existing Timing arrays. The chosen model is cleaner but requires a structural transform.

findings.title: Product type fields changed from CodeableConcept/string paths to CodeableReference-based product model

oldState.summary: R4 supplement and enteral formula product types used CodeableConcept; enteral formula product name used `baseFormulaProductName`.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 used direct codeable concepts for supplement type and base formula type, with a separately named `baseFormulaProductName`.

newState.summary: R6 supplement and enteral formula product types use CodeableReference(NutritionProduct), with enteral formula `productName`.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 can carry either a concept or a reference to a `NutritionProduct` for product-like fields. The direct concept must be nested under `concept` in JSON.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The new paths keep the same supplement/enteral formula roles and bindings, but change the data type to support references to NutritionProduct.

impact.impactRationaleMd: A raw R4 CodeableConcept at `supplement.type` or `enteralFormula.baseFormulaType` is not valid R6 CodeableReference JSON. R6 product references introduce information that R4 cannot carry in the same field. Generated models also change from a CodeableConcept property to CodeableReference.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Product identity affects dispensing, preparation, and supply-chain behavior.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of linking nutrition requests to concrete `NutritionProduct` resources is reasonable. Still, replacing existing CodeableConcept fields with `CodeableReference` and renaming enteral product paths was not the only base design available; separate optional references could have provided the new capability without invalidating old concept-shaped data.
justification.inferredGoal: Allow nutrition product fields to identify a coded class or a concrete NutritionProduct resource.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the R4 CodeableConcept product-type fields and old enteral names, and add optional NutritionProduct reference fields for concrete products.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A backward-compatible base design would keep `supplement.type`, `enteralFormula.baseFormulaType`, and `enteralFormula.baseFormulaProductName` in their R4 shapes and add optional reference elements for `NutritionProduct`. The tradeoff is a split concept/reference model and less use of the R6 `CodeableReference` idiom, but it would preserve most R4-valid instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 instances while adding product-resource expressiveness, but is less compact and less idiomatic than `CodeableReference`.

evidence.detail: R4 `supplement.type` is CodeableConcept with example binding to supplement-type.
R6 `supplement.type` is CodeableReference targeting NutritionProduct with preferred binding to supplement-type.
R4 base formula type is CodeableConcept.
R6 enteral formula type is CodeableReference targeting NutritionProduct.
R4 product name path is `baseFormulaProductName`.
R6 product name path is `productName`.

examples.examplesMd: R4 concepts can generally be nested under `CodeableReference.concept`; R6 references to NutritionProduct need policy for R4 down-conversion.

findings.narrativeMd: Nutrition product identification moved toward R6 `CodeableReference`. This allows richer product references but changes the JSON shape of existing coded values and renames the enteral base formula fields.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 CodeableConcept JSON is old-valid/new-invalid at these fields because R6 expects `concept` or `reference` children. R6 references to `NutritionProduct` are not representable in R4 without an extension or denormalizing a code/display/product name.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map R4 CodeableConcept values to `CodeableReference.concept`; map `baseFormulaProductName` to `productName`. For R6-to-R4, decide whether a NutritionProduct reference can be replaced by a code, display, and product name, or whether to preserve the reference in an extension.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Separate optional reference elements would have been more backward-compatible but less idiomatic for R6's CodeableReference pattern.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Manual review is needed where product references carry manufacturer, ingredient, or packaging detail beyond a simple code/name.

findings.title: Enteral formula additive fields moved to repeatable root `additive` backbone

oldState.summary: R4 had one optional additive type and one optional additive product name under `enteralFormula`.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 additive information was specific to enteral formula and limited to a type and product name.

newState.summary: R6 has repeatable root `additive` entries with CodeableReference modular type, product name, quantity, and route.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 additives can apply to oral diet, supplements, and/or enteral feeding and can include quantity and route.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The additive type/productName concepts are clearly related, but R6 broadens the scope beyond enteralFormula and adds new additive details.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 additive properties under `enteralFormula` are absent in R6 and must move to a different parent. R6 additives for oral diet or supplement, and R6 additive quantity/route, cannot be losslessly represented in the R4 enteral-only additive fields.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Additive quantity/type can affect nutritional composition and administration.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal is substantively broader than a rename: modular additives can apply beyond enteral formula and can carry quantity and route. Retaining the R4 enteral-only fields would reduce breakage, but it would also leave two places to express the same enteral additive and could create clinical ambiguity if both are populated. Given those material tradeoffs, the breaking normalization is probably justified.
justification.inferredGoal: Model modular additives independently of only enteral formulas.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the enteral additive fields while adding the generalized root `additive` backbone for oral diet, supplement, and enteral use.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The partial alternative is to keep `enteralFormula.additiveType` and `enteralFormula.additiveProductName` as deprecated fields while adding root `additive`. That covers old instances but risks indefinite duplicate representations and requires clear precedence/reconciliation rules.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old enteral additive data, but creates duplicate same-resource representations for enteral additives with reconciliation and safety risk.

evidence.detail: R4 additive type is under `enteralFormula`.
R4 additive product name is under `enteralFormula`.
R6 adds root repeatable `additive` backbone.
R6 additive modular type is CodeableReference(NutritionProduct).

examples.examplesMd: R6 additive details may not say whether the additive belongs to an oral diet, supplement, or enteral formula, so down-conversion can be ambiguous.

findings.narrativeMd: Additives moved from an enteral-formula-specific pair of fields to a repeatable root-level backbone. This is both a path move and a semantic broadening of what additives can attach to.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 `enteralFormula.additiveType` and `additiveProductName` are invalid R6 properties. R6 root additives with quantity, route, or non-enteral applicability are not losslessly representable in R4.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4-to-R6, create one `additive` item from the old enteral additive fields and nest the old concept under `modularType.concept`. For R6-to-R4, manually review whether each additive can safely be treated as enteral-formula additive; otherwise preserve it as an extension or do not down-convert.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The move could have been staged by retaining the old fields. The R6 design is more normalized but creates ambiguity for cross-version conversion.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: R6 does not encode in this local field alone which component the additive modifies, so implementer policy is needed for some conversions.

findings.title: `routeofAdministration` renamed to `routeOfAdministration` and widened to repeatable

oldState.summary: R4 route element was 0..1 CodeableConcept named `routeofAdministration` with extensible binding.
oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 JSON property used a lowercase `of` spelling and allowed only one route.

newState.summary: R6 route element is 0..* CodeableConcept named `routeOfAdministration` with preferred binding.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 uses camel-case `routeOfAdministration`, permits multiple routes, and weakens terminology strength to preferred.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The definitions and value set are the same route concept; the R6 path corrects camel casing and broadens cardinality.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The old JSON property name is absent in R6 and the new property is an array. R6 instances with multiple route values cannot be represented in R4's 0..1 field without choosing one or using extensions.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Route of administration can affect safe delivery.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 cardinality and binding changes are compatibility-friendly, and the multiple-route goal could have been achieved on the existing element. The breaking part is primarily the spelling/case correction, so retaining the old name with updated cardinality and definition would have been a plausible low-tradeoff base design.
justification.inferredGoal: Correct element naming and support multiple administration routes.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the R4 `routeofAdministration` spelling while widening cardinality and relaxing the binding strength.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A backward-compatible base design could keep `routeofAdministration` as the element name, change max to `*`, use the preferred binding, and clarify the definition. The downside is preserving an awkward spelling, but that is a moderate naming cost rather than a reason old instances had to become invalid.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 JSON and still supports multiple routes, but carries forward an inconsistent camelCase spelling.

evidence.detail: R4 path is `routeofAdministration`, 0..1, extensible binding to enteral-route.
R6 path is `routeOfAdministration`, 0..*, preferred binding to enteral-route.

findings.narrativeMd: The route field changed spelling and became repeatable. This is easy to miss because the semantic label is almost unchanged, but strict parsers and generated classes treat it as a different property.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 `routeofAdministration` is old-valid/new-invalid. R6 multiple routes are not representable in the R4 single route field without loss.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rename the property to `routeOfAdministration` and wrap the value in an array. On down-conversion, choose a primary route only if a clinical policy exists; otherwise use an extension or manual review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The case-correcting rename could have been avoided by preserving the old spelling. However, the R6 spelling is more consistent with FHIR naming conventions.

findings.title: `maxVolumeToDeliver` renamed to `maxVolumeToAdminister`

oldState.summary: R4 optional max volume field was named `maxVolumeToDeliver`.

newState.summary: R6 optional max volume field is named `maxVolumeToAdminister`.

facts.note: Quantity profile widening is covered in the quantity-profile finding.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: Both fields represent the upper limit on formula feeding volume over a period and share cardinality and Quantity type.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Instances with the old property name must be transformed. Generated code and FHIRPath rules using `maxVolumeToDeliver` will not find the R6 field.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Max volume is a safety-relevant dosing limit for enteral feeding.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The semantic clarification is understandable, but the R4 definition already described the maximum quantity administered to the subject. Because the same clinical meaning could be expressed by improving the definition while retaining the element name, the property-level break was probably avoidable.
justification.inferredGoal: Use terminology that emphasizes administration rather than supply delivery.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `maxVolumeToDeliver` and clarify in the definition that the limit is on administered volume.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would keep `enteralFormula.maxVolumeToDeliver`, update the short/definition text to emphasize administration, and apply any Quantity widening separately. That avoids duplicate fields and preserves existing instances, with only a naming-precision tradeoff.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old path compatibility, but retains wording that is less precise than `maxVolumeToAdminister`.

evidence.detail: R4 defines max volume under `maxVolumeToDeliver`.
R6 defines max volume under `maxVolumeToAdminister`.

findings.narrativeMd: The enteral feeding maximum-volume field was renamed. Although the meaning is close, strict JSON processing and generated models require a direct transform.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `maxVolumeToDeliver` are invalid in R6 until the field is renamed. R6 values can generally be represented in R4 after renaming, subject to the R4 SimpleQuantity restriction reported separately.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rename the field and test conversions involving volume limits because missed max-volume data can alter delivery safeguards.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A deprecated alias would have avoided the break, but the R6 name is clearer about administration.

findings.title: `oralDiet.fluidConsistencyType` was removed

oldState.summary: R4 had repeatable CodeableConcept `fluidConsistencyType` for required liquid/fluid consistency.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 modeled fluid consistency separately from solid-food texture.

newState.summary: R6 has no `fluidConsistencyType`; oral texture definitions now mention solid and/or liquid texture modifications.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 appears to fold liquid texture concepts into the broader `oralDiet.texture` model, but no explicit one-to-one computable mapping is present in the StructureDefinition.

facts.note: Possible but not proven equivalent from the StructureDefinitions.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: R6 texture text refers to solid and/or liquid modifications, but the old fluid-specific path and value set are absent.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Any R4 instance with fluid consistency content has an absent path in R6. The migration is clinically material because liquid consistency is safety-relevant and there is no computable ConceptMap in the supplied inputs.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Fluid consistency is relevant to dysphagia and aspiration-risk workflows.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Unifying solid and liquid texture handling may be clinically reasonable, but the supplied definitions do not prove that R4 liquid-consistency codes map cleanly to the R6 texture structure. Removing the field without a clear base replacement or computable mapping is safety-sensitive and not clearly justified.
justification.inferredGoal: Possibly unify texture handling for solids and liquids.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `fluidConsistencyType` as a deprecated base element while broadening `oralDiet.texture` to cover liquid texture.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The partial base-design alternative is to retain `oralDiet.fluidConsistencyType` as deprecated while allowing liquid texture in `oralDiet.texture`. A ConceptMap would help migration, but it is not itself a backward-compatible base design. The retained-field option reduces breakage but risks indefinite duplicate liquid-texture representations.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves explicit liquid-consistency data, but creates duplicate paths for liquid texture and needs safety-sensitive reconciliation rules.

evidence.detail: R4 defines repeatable `fluidConsistencyType` bound to ValueSet/consistency-type.
No R6 `NutritionOrder.oralDiet.fluidConsistencyType` element was found.
R6 texture definition refers to foods `i.e. solid and/or liquid`.
evidence.quote: Class that describes any texture modifications in addition to the oral diet type required for the patient to safely consume various types of foods (i.e. solid and/or liquid).

examples.examplesMd: Mapping this example to R6 likely requires `oralDiet.texture`, but the correct code and target field should be terminology-reviewed.

findings.narrativeMd: The fluid-consistency field is gone. Because fluid thickness can be clinically important, this is more than a cosmetic model change; it risks losing safety-relevant diet texture information unless mapped carefully.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `oralDiet.fluidConsistencyType` are invalid in R6. R6 may represent similar meaning through texture, but that is not a guaranteed round-trip without terminology mapping.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not drop this field. Build a reviewed mapping from R4 `consistency-type` concepts to R6 texture representation, and include test cases for thin, nectar-thick, honey-thick, and pudding-thick fluids if used locally.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A deprecated fluid-specific element or an official ConceptMap would have reduced risk. Without that, migration requires site-specific clinical terminology review.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: This finding has high clinical significance but medium mapping certainty because the official narrative implementation notes and terminology expansions were not compared.

findings.title: `oralDiet.texture.foodType` renamed to `oralDiet.texture.type`

oldState.summary: R4 optional texture target food type path was `foodType`.

newState.summary: R6 optional texture target food type path is `type` with preferred binding.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element keeps cardinality, type, value set, and role, with a shorter R6 name.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The old child name is not valid R6. The binding strength increase is conformance-relevant but not a hard validation break because preferred bindings do not require membership.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Target food type affects how texture modifications are applied.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The binding and definition changes can be applied without renaming the element. Since `foodType` already described the target of the texture modification and could be broadened to solid or liquid food types, the path rename to `type` was probably avoidable.
justification.inferredGoal: Use shorter naming inside an already food-related texture backbone.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `oralDiet.texture.foodType` while updating its binding strength and definition for the broader solid-or-liquid texture context.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would keep `texture.foodType`, use the R6 preferred binding if desired, and clarify that it covers the food or liquid type affected by the texture modification. The tradeoff is only naming neatness within the backbone.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old instances and APIs, but keeps a longer, less streamlined name inside the texture backbone.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `foodType` 0..1 CodeableConcept bound to modified-foodtype.
R6 defines `type` 0..1 CodeableConcept bound to modified-foodtype.

findings.narrativeMd: The food type to which a texture modification applies changed child name from `foodType` to `type`. This is localized but breaks serializers and FHIRPath expressions that reference the old child.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 `texture.foodType` is invalid in R6. The value can generally be copied to R6 `texture.type` without semantic loss.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rename `foodType` to `type` in each `oralDiet.texture` entry and update generated model references and query paths.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This rename was avoidable from a compatibility standpoint, but the shorter name is understandable within the context of the texture backbone.

findings.title: R4 SimpleQuantity profiles removed from several Quantity elements

affectedLocation.newPath: Corresponding R6 Quantity elements, including renamed fields

oldState.summary: R4 constrained multiple Quantity elements to the SimpleQuantity profile.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 Quantity fields such as nutrient amount, supplement quantity, caloric density, administration quantity, rateQuantity, and max volume used the SimpleQuantity profile.

newState.summary: R6 uses unconstrained Quantity at those corresponding fields and new Quantity fields.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 no longer locally profiles these Quantity fields as SimpleQuantity, allowing a broader Quantity domain.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not an R4-to-R6 validation break because R6 widens the type. It is a codegen and down-conversion risk: R6 Quantity values using features disallowed by R4 SimpleQuantity may be rejected by R4 validators or R4 generated models.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Quantity interpretation affects dosing, volume limits, and nutrient amounts.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: This is not a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design change because values valid under the R4 SimpleQuantity profile remain valid when R6 accepts the broader Quantity type. The only material issue is that new R6 Quantity features may not down-convert cleanly to R4.
justification.inferredGoal: Allow the full Quantity datatype for nutrition quantities.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: widening from SimpleQuantity-profiled Quantity to unconstrained Quantity preserves R4-valid Quantity instances.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No backward-compatible alternative is needed for forward compatibility. Keeping the SimpleQuantity profile would be a down-conversion-oriented constraint, not a less-breaking way to preserve R4 instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 design is needed; retaining SimpleQuantity would mainly improve R6-to-R4 down-conversion while reducing R6 expressiveness.

evidence.detail: R4 has SimpleQuantity profile.
R6 has unprofiled Quantity.
R4 has SimpleQuantity profile.
R6 has unprofiled Quantity.
R4 rateQuantity uses SimpleQuantity profile.
R6 rate[x] Quantity has no SimpleQuantity profile.

examples.examplesMd: The example illustrates a broader Quantity feature that may not satisfy an R4 SimpleQuantity profile.

findings.narrativeMd: Several local Quantity fields were widened by dropping the R4 SimpleQuantity profile. This is not a forward validation break, but it matters for generated types and R6-to-R4 conversion.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-valid SimpleQuantity values remain acceptable in R6. R6-valid Quantity values that use non-simple features may fail R4 validation when mapped back to R4 fields that were profiled as SimpleQuantity.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4 conversion, validate each Quantity against the R4 SimpleQuantity profile and either normalize, reject, or preserve non-simple details via extension. Include comparator and unusual unit cases in tests.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This is a safe widening for R4-to-R6 but not for round-tripping. Keeping SimpleQuantity would have maximized down-conversion but limited R6 expressiveness.

findings.title: Nutrition-specific terminology bindings became preferred and some value sets changed

affectedLocation.oldPath: NutritionOrder.foodPreferenceModifier | excludeFoodModifier | oralDiet.type | oralDiet.nutrient.modifier | oralDiet.texture.modifier | supplement.type | enteralFormula.baseFormulaType | enteralFormula.additiveType

oldState.summary: R4 mostly used example bindings for nutrition concepts, with enteral route extensible.

binding.description: Representative R4 nutrition bindings included encounter-diet, food-type, diet-type, nutrient-code, texture-code, supplement-type, entformula-type, and entformula-additive.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 nutrition concept bindings were generally loose example bindings, except `enteralFormula.routeofAdministration` was extensible.

newState.summary: R6 changes many local nutrition concept bindings to preferred and replaces some value sets.

binding.description: R6 uses preferred bindings for many nutrition concept fields and introduces edible-substance-type plus SNOMED-based additive/formula value set changes.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 encourages the specified value sets more strongly and changes several value set definitions, but preferred bindings still do not make non-member codes invalid.

facts.newValue: SNOMED CT-based compose plus explicit SNOMED concepts

impact.impactRationaleMd: Preferred bindings do not make old codes invalid, so this is not a hard instance break. It can still affect conformance scoring, terminology validation warnings, analytics, and round-trip expectations because several value set definitions and code systems changed.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Terminology shifts can affect diet preparation, allergies/preferences, and interoperability.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Moving many nutrition concept bindings from example to preferred is a modest conformance tightening rather than a hard validation break, and the interoperability goal is reasonable. The exact code-level impact is still limited by absent expansions or ConceptMaps, but preferred bindings are a relatively low-breakage way to signal stronger terminology expectations.
justification.inferredGoal: Improve interoperability by preferring more specific nutrition value sets.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep example binding strength in the base resource while publishing the R6 value sets as recommendations or profile requirements.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The partial base-design alternative is to retain example bindings and move stronger terminology expectations into profiles or guidance. Guidance and ConceptMaps alone are migration aids, not a `Yes` alternative; the actual less-breaking base choice would be weaker binding strength, which only incompletely meets the interoperability goal.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves weaker legacy terminology expectations, but provides less computable pressure toward interoperable nutrition coding.

evidence.detail: R4 binds foodPreferenceModifier to encounter-diet with example strength.
R6 binds foodPreferenceModifier to edible-substance-type with preferred strength.
R4 binds excludeFoodModifier to food-type with example strength.
R6 binds excludeFoodModifier to edible-substance-type with preferred strength.
R4 compose uses the HL7 entformula-additive code system, while R6 compose is SNOMED CT-based with explicit SNOMED concepts; no expansion was present.
R6 nutrient-code contains a larger explicit SNOMED concept list than R4 in local compose data; no expansion was present.

examples.examplesMd: No old-valid/new-invalid JSON example is shown because preferred/example bindings are not hard validation restrictions. The migration issue is terminology quality and semantic mapping.

findings.narrativeMd: Many nutrition concept bindings moved from loose example bindings to preferred bindings, and some value sets changed identity or composition. This will not generally reject old instances, but it can change validation warnings, terminology mapping, and what codes are considered interoperable.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances remain syntactically valid after structural migration even if their codes are outside the R6 preferred value set. However, terminology services, analytics, and profile conformance may flag or normalize them differently. R6-preferred codes may not map cleanly to R4's older example value sets.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Run terminology analysis separately for locally used diet, supplement, additive, nutrient, texture, and edible-substance codes. Where possible, maintain ConceptMaps from R4-era code systems/value sets to R6-preferred SNOMED-based sets.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Keeping example bindings would be more backward-compatible but weaker for interoperability. Preferred bindings are a relatively non-breaking way to encourage convergence, but value set replacements still need migration guidance.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Confidence is limited by the absence of terminology expansions and official ConceptMaps in the checked inputs.

findings.title: Required `status` and `intent` bindings changed by adding R6 request codes

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 status codes were draft, active, on-hold, revoked, completed, entered-in-error, unknown. R4 intent codes did not include solicit-offer or offer-response.

newState.summary: R6 required request-status|6.0.0-ballot4 and request-intent|6.0.0-ballot4, adding codes and changing some definitions.

changedCodes.changeSummary: Definition now refers to authorization by the requestor rather than specifically a Practitioner.
Definition no longer says legally binding.
Definition refers to RequestOrchestration rather than RequestGroup.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: Compared local CodeSystem concept lists, not live terminology expansions.

newState.narrativeMd: The R6 required bindings preserve all R4 codes checked locally, but add `status=ended` and `intent=solicit-offer`/`offer-response`, and adjust several request-intent definitions.

impact.impactRationaleMd: No R4 request-status or request-intent code was removed in the local CodeSystem comparison, so this is not an R4-to-R6 hard break. R6 instances using the added required-binding codes cannot be validly represented in R4 without mapping or extension.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Workflow status and intent drive order processing and validity.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The added request lifecycle and offer/response codes increase R6 expressiveness without invalidating existing R4 `status` or `intent` codes. Definition changes may affect business rules, but the primary compatibility risk is for older R4 receivers that cannot represent new R6 codes.
justification.inferredGoal: Evolve common request lifecycle and offer/response workflow semantics.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the required status and intent value sets were expanded rather than narrowed, so R4 codes remain valid in R6.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No R4-to-R6 backward-compatible alternative is applicable. Official ConceptMaps or extensions can mitigate R6-to-R4 conversion, but they are conversion aids rather than evidence that the R6 base value sets should avoid additive codes.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: New R6 codes need R6-to-R4 mapping policy, but that is a down-conversion issue rather than a less-breaking R6 base design.

evidence.detail: R4 status has required binding to request-status|4.0.1.
R6 status has required binding to request-status|6.0.0-ballot4.
Local CodeSystem comparison found added R6 code `ended` and no removed R4 status codes.
Local CodeSystem comparison found added R6 codes `solicit-offer` and `offer-response`, with definition changes for `order`, `directive`, and `option`.

examples.examplesMd: This fragment focuses on required terminology. A full R6 instance would also include `subject`, `dateTime`, and nutrition content.

findings.narrativeMd: The required workflow terminology evolved. Existing R4 status/intent codes remain available in R6, but R6 can now express workflow states/intents that R4 cannot validate as required-binding codes.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation is safe for the checked status/intent codes. R6-to-R4 validation fails for added R6 codes unless mapped to an R4 code or preserved outside the base element.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4, define mappings for `ended`, `solicit-offer`, and `offer-response` or reject them when no safe R4 equivalent exists. Review business logic that assumes `order` always implies a Practitioner-authorized request or that `directive` is legally binding.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The added codes are forward-compatible but not round-trip compatible. Official ConceptMaps would be the least disruptive support for older systems.

findings.title: Several new optional R6 fields create R6-to-R4 representability gaps

affectedLocation.newPath: NutritionOrder.basedOn | groupIdentifier | priority | supportingInformation | performer | outsideFoodAllowed | enteralFormula.deliveryDevice[x] | oralDiet.caloricDensity | supplement.caloricDensity

oldState.summary: R4 had no direct local elements for these fields.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 NutritionOrder lacks the R6 workflow links, group identifier, priority, supporting information, intended performer, outside-food allowance, enteral delivery-device choice, and oral/supplement caloric-density fields listed here.

newState.summary: R6 adds optional workflow, performer, device, calorie, and policy fields.
newState.narrativeMd: The fields are optional, so they do not break R4 instances moving forward, but they matter for R6 records sent to R4 systems.

impact.impactRationaleMd: These additions are optional and therefore not hard breaking for R4-to-R6 validation. They create meaningful data-loss risk in down-conversion because R4 has no same-path elements for the added workflow, device, performer, policy, and calorie data.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Loss of performer, priority, support data, or delivery device can affect operations and administration.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Optional additions are the normal backward-compatible way to add workflow, performer, device, calorie-density, and policy details. This finding is mainly an R6-to-R4 representability concern, not evidence of a breaking R4-to-R6 base design.
justification.inferredGoal: Add workflow/context and richer nutrition details to NutritionOrder.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the listed R6 elements are optional additions and do not invalidate R4 NutritionOrder instances.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base alternative is needed because old instances remain valid without the new elements. Cross-version extensions or explicit loss policy can support down-conversion, but those are mitigations rather than base-design alternatives.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Adds R6 expressiveness at the cost of R4 round-trip fidelity; older-receiver handling is conversion policy, not a base-design alternative.

evidence.detail: R6 adds `basedOn` 0..* Reference(CarePlan|NutritionOrder|ServiceRequest|RequestOrchestration).
R6 adds `performer` 0..* CodeableReference with multiple performer targets.
R6 adds deliveryDevice[x] as CodeableConcept or canonical(DeviceDefinition).
R6 adds outsideFoodAllowed boolean.
No corresponding R4 NutritionOrder local elements were found for these R6 additions.

examples.examplesMd: The example uses R6-only fields. R4 can preserve them only via extensions or external metadata.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds several optional but operationally meaningful fields. They do not make old R4 instances invalid, but R6 records using them lose information when sent to R4 systems unless a cross-version extension policy exists.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 is unaffected because the fields are optional. R6-to-R4 is lossy for populated fields: R4 has no direct elements for intended performer, priority, delivery device, outside-food policy, and several workflow/context fields.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For down-conversion, define which fields are dropped, extension-preserved, or mapped to external workflow records. Include tests for deliveryDevice[x] canonical references and CodeableReference performer values.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Adding optional fields is the backward-compatible design for forward migration. The unavoidable issue is that older R4 receivers cannot understand the new fields without extensions.

findings.title: `enteralFormula.administrationInstruction` primitive type changed from string to markdown

impact.impactRationaleMd: FHIR JSON still carries a primitive string value, so ordinary R4 string content should remain representable in R6. The risk is generated-code and display behavior: markdown-aware renderers may interpret formatting, while R4 clients may display markdown syntax literally.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Instruction rendering can affect readability, but this change alone does not alter structured dosing.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The type change supports richer formatted feeding instructions while preserving the string-like JSON representation. Existing R4 primitive values remain representable, so the compatibility issue is primarily code generation or rendering behavior rather than old-valid/new-invalid instances.
justification.inferredGoal: Allow richer formatted free-text enteral feeding instructions.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: `markdown` remains serialized as a JSON string, so R4 string values remain wire-compatible in R6.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No R4-to-R6 backward-compatible alternative is required. Keeping `string` would reduce type churn but would also fail to signal markdown-capable rendering; it is not needed to preserve R4 instance validity.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6 gains formatted-text signaling; generated types and renderers may need updates, but this is not a base instance break.

evidence.detail: R4 type code is `string`.
R6 type code is `markdown`.

enteralFormula.administrationInstruction: Increase rate every 2 hours as tolerated.

examples.examplesMd: Existing plain string values can usually be copied. Markdown-specific formatting should be display-tested.

findings.narrativeMd: The free-text enteral administration instruction now has markdown type. The JSON primitive shape remains string-like, but typed clients and renderers need to account for markdown semantics.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: This is not expected to make ordinary R4 string values invalid in R6. It can still break generated code that distinguishes string and markdown primitive wrappers, and R6 markdown content may not render as intended in R4 clients.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Copy plain strings directly, but update code generation, UI rendering, and sanitization paths for markdown. Test markdown punctuation, line breaks, and any local rich-text behavior.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Using markdown is mostly compatible at the wire level, but not necessarily at the generated-type or rendering level.
